newsitem.title: CYPRUS: FEATURE - Cyprus bourse sees bright prospects in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cyprus bourse sees bright prospects in 1997.

text.p: It started out as an unofficial over-the-counter exchange racing to record-high gains in the first two months of 1996 and came down to earth with a bump after an official framework was set up.

The Cyprus Stock Exchange (CSE) closed the year with losses of 17.75 percent in the now regulated exchange that opened on March 29 after years of trading that was not controlled by any regulatory authority.

In anticipation of the official framework, trading volume swelled in the first two months of the year, with many stocks reaching record highs and daily transactions averaging between two million and three million pounds ($4.2 million-$6.4 million).
But gains shrank and volume plummeted when the 41-share bourse started official operations at the end of March.

"We will never see what happened in the first two months of the year happen again," CSE director Nondas Metaxas told Reuters. "There was a necessary correction - 1996 was a very satisfactory year for us."
Sometimes up to five months would pass before an investor would get his share certificate under the previous exchange, Metaxas said.
TAKING CARE OF BUSINESS

One of the pressing tasks the CSE needed to address was clearing up the mess left behind by the previous system. The bourse was forced to close for two weeks before its official opening in March for companies to settle title issues.
"That was a dreadful mistake," said Nicolas Severis, chairman of Sigma-Severis and Athientis Securities based in Nicosia.
"As far as foreign investors were concerned it was like a bank closing - freezing of assets."
Domestically, a different problem arose for investors, who did not have their titles even after the two-week period lapsed.
"Eventually they got their shares but by then the market started declining so they were not prepared to sell," Severis said.
In June the island's central bank increased the maximum holding a foreign investor could have in a publicly quoted company to 49 percent from the previous ceiling of 25 percent.
A ceiling of 15 percent still exists for the banking sectors, which absorbs more than 50 percent of daily transactions on the CSE.
Though official figures are not available due to the lack of a central registry, Metaxas says foreign interest is strong.
"The interest is there judging by the visits and queries we are getting from foreigners and representatives of serious organisations," he said.
FUTURE PROSPECTS LIE WITH NEW ISSUES
During the last few months the performance of the exchange has been slow, an observation many floor players have put down to either lack of investor interest or empty pockets.
"In essence people have lost interest in existing issues and until such time as the market broadens they are not going to be too enthusiastic," said Severis.
The central bank is expected to float five-year government development bonds on the market in the first six months of 1997.

"That is going to drive the market in 1997," said Severis, adding that further listings were expected by Cypriot companies and possibly Greek ones. The CSE accepts smaller companies than the Athens bourse, making it attractive to some Greek firms trying to get listed.
CSE PLANS
The CSE is pressing ahead with its target of full automation within the next 18 months, said Metaxas.

The settlement period, currently at nine days or "T+9" will remain in place until automation is completed. "Then the settlement period will definitely be lowered, to three or to zero because the system will be dematerialised," he said.
In March the floor will move from its cramped premises in the Cyprus Chamber of Commerce and Industry to more spacious surroundings in a nearby building.
Another target that appears to have become bogged down in red tape is leglislation making insider trading a crime.
"In my opinion it is a serious drawback," Metaxas said. "The existing regulations are limited in power and do not make it a criminal offence nor does it define it."
But the lack of legislation has not discouraged investors, he said. "I don't think it is an obstacle, but it may be something which would make us feel more comfortable."
